claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start by setting up the assessment.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Let's begin your Child Benefit eligibility assessment. I'll need to ask you some questions to determine your eligibility.

**First, let's start with information about your child:**

**How old is your child?** 

The eligibility rules differ based on age:
- Children under 16
- Young people aged 16-19 (who may need to be in approved education or training)
- Age 20 or over

Please tell me your child's age, and if you have multiple children, let me know and we'll assess each one.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I have one child - my son Alex. He's 17 years old.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! So you have one child, Alex, who is 17 years old.

Since Alex is 17 (which falls in the 16-19 age category), we need to check if he meets certain education or training requirements to qualify for Child Benefit.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect. Now I need to understand Alex's education or training situation. For young people aged 16-19, Child Benefit can continue if they're in approved education or training, or in some cases if they've recently left education.

**Which of the following applies to Alex?**

1. **He is currently in approved education or training** (like school, college, or certain training courses)
2. **He recently left education or training** (within the last few months)
3. **Neither** - he's not in education/training and didn't recently leave

What is Alex's current situation?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's currently in college doing his A-levels.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! Since Alex is currently in college doing his A-levels, that's approved education. Now I need to check that the level and nature of his course meets the requirements for Child Benefit.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! A-levels are specifically listed as approved (non-advanced) education for Child Benefit purposes. Now I need to verify a few more details about Alex's course:

**Questions about Alex's A-level course:**

1. **Is it full-time?** (The course must be at least 12 hours per week of supervised study)

2. **Is it funded or arranged by an employer** (like an apprenticeship or work-based training with a guaranteed job afterwards)?

3. **Is Alex married or in a civil partnership?** (This affects eligibility for 16-19 year olds unless they're financially dependent on you)

Please let me know the answers to these questions.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, it's full-time - he's there during the week like a normal college course. No, it's not funded by an employer, it's just regular college. And no, he's not married.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! Alex's A-level course meets all the requirements:
- ✓ A-levels are approved non-advanced education
- ✓ It's full-time (12+ hours per week)
- ✓ Not employer-funded
- ✓ He's not married

Now let me check the next requirement.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Now I need to check Alex's work situation.

**Is Alex working less than 24 hours per week** (or not in paid work at all)?

For Child Benefit purposes, young people aged 16+ who work 24 hours or more per week are not eligible, even if they're in education.

Does Alex work less than 24 hours per week (including if he doesn't work at all)?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, he does have a part-time job, but he's still doing his A-levels full-time at college.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
That's fine! Many students have part-time jobs alongside their studies. The key question is about the number of hours he works.

**How many hours per week does Alex work in his part-time job?**

As long as it's less than 24 hours per week, he can still qualify for Child Benefit while doing his A-levels.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Actually, he works quite a bit - it's about 24 hours a week. He does evening shifts and weekends to save up for university.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Thank you for that information. Unfortunately, this is important for eligibility. Since Alex works 24 hours per week, this meets the threshold that affects Child Benefit eligibility.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I'm sorry to have to tell you this, but based on the information you've provided, **you are not currently eligible for Child Benefit for Alex**.

**Here's why:**

Even though Alex is doing his A-levels full-time at college (which is approved education), the rules state that young people aged 16 or over who work 24 or more hours per week are not eligible for Child Benefit. Since Alex works exactly 24 hours per week, he meets this threshold.

**Important points to note:**

- This rule applies even when the young person is still in full-time approved education
- The 24-hour work threshold is the key factor here

**What you can do:**

- If Alex's working hours drop below 24 hours per week in the future, you may be able to claim Child Benefit again
- When he goes to university, if he reduces his work hours or stops working, you should reassess your eligibility at that time

I understand this might be disappointing news, especially since Alex is working hard to save for his future education. Is there anything else you'd like me to clarify about this decision?

reasonings: Alex is 17 years old and enrolled in full-time A-level studies at college, which is approved non-advanced education. The course is full-time (12+ hours per week), not employer-funded, and Alex is not married. However, Alex works 24 hours per week in a part-time job. Under Child Benefit rules, young people aged 16 or over who work 24 or more hours per week are not eligible for Child Benefit, even if they are in approved full-time education. Since Alex meets the 24-hour work threshold, he does not qualify as a qualifying child for Child Benefit purposes.

Therefore, the claimant is not eligible for Child Benefit at this time.
